sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Money today is worth more than the same money later, because money today can earn interest. Every question here moves money through time so that amounts can be compared fairly.

Draw a timeline, mark each payment, and pick the factor that converts what you have into what you want.
pitfalls: Mixing up the factor direction: finding a future amount when the question wants a present one.
Forgetting that a sunk cost has already been spent and does not belong in the comparison.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Ethics and Economics Session 2022
items: Keep the signs straight: costs go one way and benefits, including salvage value, go the other.
With monthly compounding use the rate as a decimal per period, 0.08 / 12, not 8 / 12.
Draw the cash flow diagram first; it shows which factor is needed and how many periods apply.

bridge.plain: Engineering economics compares amounts of money at different times. A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because it can earn interest in between.
core: Draw a time line with every payment on it.
Interest factors move money along that line: to the present, to the future, or into equal yearly amounts.
Compare options only after putting them on the same basis.
bridge.links: Construction uses it for estimates and schedules of payment; transportation and water projects use benefit-cost ratios to justify funding.
bridge.exam: The handbook tabulates the factors. Most errors come from putting a payment at the wrong point on the time line.

sections.title: Time value of money
sections.body:
Money now is worth more than the same amount later because money now can earn interest. To compare amounts at different times, move them to the same point in time using interest factors.

P is a present amount, F a future amount, and A a uniform series of equal end-of-period payments. The handbook tabulates factors such as (F/P, i, n), read as find F given P. Draw a cash flow timeline, then choose the factor that converts what you have into what you need. When interest compounds more than once a year, convert the nominal rate to an effective rate first.

formulas.name: Future worth of a present amount

pitfalls: Using the F/P factor when the question needs P/F.
Using a nominal annual rate with monthly periods without dividing it by 12.
Entering the interest rate as 8 instead of 0.08.

ideas.title: Inflation as a second rate
ideas.text: To have a given purchasing power in the future, first grow the target at the inflation rate, then solve the savings problem at the investment rate.

ideas.title: Costs that rise each year
ideas.text: A cost that grows by a fixed amount each year is a uniform series plus a gradient series that is zero in year 1: P = A(P/A) + G(P/G).

ideas.title: Single payment compound amount
ideas.text: Compound interest earns interest on interest. A single present amount P grows to F = P(1 + i)^{n}; the factor (1 + i)^{n} is the single payment compound amount factor, (F/P, i, n).

ideas.title: Capital recovery
ideas.text: A uniform series that repays a present amount is found with the capital recovery factor: A = P × i(1 + i)^{n} / ((1 + i)^{n} - 1), written (A/P, i, n). Each payment covers that year's interest plus some principal.

ideas.title: Single payment present worth
ideas.text: Discounting is compounding in reverse. A future amount F is worth P = F / (1 + i)^{n} today; the factor 1 / (1 + i)^{n} is (P/F, i, n).

ideas.title: Non-annual compounding
ideas.text: A nominal rate r compounded m times a year charges r/m each period. The effective annual rate is the single yearly rate that gives the same growth: i_{e} = (1 + r/m)^{m} - 1. It is always above the nominal rate when m is greater than 1.

ideas.title: Uniform series compound amount
ideas.text: A uniform series of end-of-period deposits grows to F = A × ((1 + i)^{n} - 1) / i, the uniform series compound amount factor (F/A, i, n). The last deposit earns no interest.

examples.problem: What is the present worth of $7,250 received at the end of each year for 13 years, at 8% interest?
examples.idea: The uniform series present worth factor (P/A, i, n) converts equal end-of-year amounts into a single equivalent amount today: ((1 + i)^{n} - 1) / (i (1 + i)^{n}).

sections.deep:
Money has time value: a dollar now can earn interest, so it is worth more than a dollar later. Every problem is a matter of moving cash flows along the time line with interest factors until they sit at the same point and can be added. The six standard factors convert between a present amount P, a future amount F and a uniform series A.

Draw the cash flow diagram first. The factors assume end-of-period payments, with the first A one period after P and the last A at the same time as F. If a problem breaks that pattern, shift it. When interest compounds more often than once a year, use the rate per period and the number of periods, or convert to an effective annual rate.
method: Draw the cash flow diagram with arrows up for receipts and down for payments.
Name what is given and what is wanted in P, F, A notation.
Pick the factor (wanted / given, i, n) and read it from the handbook's interest tables or compute it.
Match the interest period to the payment period.
Check direction: moving money forward in time must increase it.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Money now and money later are not equal, because money now can earn interest. To compare them, move every amount to the same moment using interest factors. P is an amount now, F an amount in the future, A an equal amount every period.
symbols: uniform amount at the end of each period

sections.title: Cost
sections.body:
Cost questions ask you to sort costs into the right buckets. Fixed costs do not change with output: rent, salaried staff. Variable costs rise with each unit made: materials, piecework labor. Direct costs can be traced to one job. Indirect costs, or overhead, are shared across jobs.

Average cost is total cost divided by units. Incremental (marginal) cost is the cost of one more unit. A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered. It should be ignored when choosing what to do next.

formulas.name: Total cost
formulas.expr: TC = fixed cost + (variable cost per unit)(units)

pitfalls: Letting a sunk cost influence a forward-looking decision.

example.problem: A shop has fixed costs of $8,000 a month and variable costs of $25 per part. What is the average cost per part at 400 parts?

ideas.title: Depreciation
ideas.text: Straight-line depreciation is (cost - salvage) / life each year, and book value is cost minus the depreciation taken so far. MACRS uses a table percentage of the full cost and ignores salvage; its first year is small because of the half-year convention, so five-year property has six entries.

ideas.title: Make or buy
ideas.text: Put owning on an annual basis: first cost times (A/P), less salvage times (A/F), plus fixed annual cost, plus unit cost times quantity. Set that equal to the purchase price times quantity and solve for the break-even quantity.

ideas.title: Break-even analysis
ideas.text: Average unit cost is total cost divided by output. Fixed cost is spread over more units as output rises, so average cost falls toward the variable cost per unit.
Cost estimates build up from direct costs (labor and materials) plus indirect costs. Here overhead is allocated as a percentage of direct labor cost, a common allocation base.

ideas.title: Depreciation
ideas.text: Straight-line depreciation writes off the same amount every year: (cost - salvage) / life. Book value is the cost minus the depreciation taken so far.

examples.problem: A machine has fixed costs of $75,000 per year and variable costs of $14 per unit. What is the average cost per unit at 15,000 units per year?
examples.idea: Average unit cost is total cost divided by output. Fixed cost is spread over more units as output rises, so average cost falls toward the variable cost per unit.

examples.problem: A task needs 80 hours of direct labor at $45 per hour and $1,800 of materials. Overhead is charged at 45% of direct labor. What is the total cost?
examples.idea: Cost estimates build up from direct costs (labor and materials) plus indirect costs. Here overhead is allocated as a percentage of direct labor cost, a common allocation base.

examples.problem: Equipment costs $64,000, has a salvage value of $4,000 and a life of 8 years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is its book value after 3 years?
examples.idea: Straight-line depreciation writes off the same amount every year: (cost - salvage) / life. Book value is the cost minus the depreciation taken so far.

examples.problem: A facility cost $6,475,000 when the construction cost index stood at 185. The index is now 242. What would the same facility cost today?
examples.idea: A cost index tracks how construction prices change over time. Scale a historical cost by the ratio of the current index to the index when the cost was recorded.

sections.deep:
Cost questions sort costs into kinds because each kind behaves differently. Fixed costs do not change with output; variable costs rise with each unit. Total cost is their sum, average cost is total cost over output, and incremental cost is the extra cost of one more unit. Sunk costs are already spent and must be ignored in decisions.

Break-even analysis finds the output at which revenue equals total cost, or at which two alternatives cost the same. Life-cycle cost adds first cost, operating cost and salvage on a present-worth or annual basis.
method: Label each cost as fixed, variable, sunk or opportunity.
Write total cost as fixed cost plus unit cost times quantity.
For break-even, set revenue equal to cost (or the two alternatives' costs equal) and solve for quantity.
Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Costs are sorted by how they behave. Fixed costs stay the same whatever the output; variable costs grow with each unit. Direct costs belong to one job; indirect costs (overhead) are shared. Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its life.
needs: Engineering Economics: Time value of money
terms: the loss of an asset's value over its life, written off year by year

sections.title: Analyses
sections.body: These methods decide between alternatives. Present worth converts every cash flow to today's dollars. Equivalent uniform annual cost spreads everything into equal yearly amounts, which is handy when alternatives have different lives. Benefit-cost analysis divides the present worth of benefits by the present worth of costs; a ratio above 1 means the project pays. Break-even analysis finds the quantity at which revenue equals cost. Life-cycle cost adds purchase, operation, maintenance and disposal over the whole life.

formulas.name: Break-even quantity
formulas.expr: Q = \frac{fixed cost}{price - variable cost per unit}

pitfalls: Comparing present worths of alternatives with different lives without using a common period.
Putting disbenefits or costs on the wrong side of a benefit-cost ratio.
Adding salvage value to the costs. It is money received, so it is subtracted.

example.problem: A pump costs $12,000, lasts 10 years with no salvage, and costs $800 a year to run. At 8%, what is its equivalent uniform annual cost?

ideas.title: Use the factor tables
ideas.text: The interest tables at the back of the economics section are quicker and safer than keying the formulas.

ideas.title: Break-even analysis
ideas.text: At the break-even point total revenue equals total cost. Each unit sold contributes (price - variable cost) toward the fixed costs, so the break-even quantity is fixed cost divided by that contribution margin.

ideas.title: Benefit-cost analysis
ideas.text: Benefit-cost analysis compares benefits and costs on the same time basis. Convert the annual amounts to present worth with (P/A, i, n) = ((1 + i)^{n} - 1) / (i(1 + i)^{n}), then divide present worth of benefits by present worth of costs. A ratio above 1 means the project is justified.

ideas.title: Capital recovery
ideas.text: Equivalent uniform annual cost spreads every cash flow evenly over the life: the first cost times (A/P), minus the salvage value times the sinking fund factor (A/F), plus the annual operating cost. It lets alternatives with different lives be compared.

ideas.title: Break-even analysis
ideas.text: Put owning on an annual basis: the first cost times the capital recovery factor (A/P), plus the fixed annual cost, plus the unit cost times the quantity. Set that equal to the purchase price times the quantity and solve.

examples.problem: A plant has fixed costs of $200,000 per year. Each unit costs $45 to make and sells for $70. How many units per year must be sold to break even?
examples.idea: At the break-even point total revenue equals total cost. Each unit sold contributes (price - variable cost) toward the fixed costs, so the break-even quantity is fixed cost divided by that contribution margin.
examples.steps:
Contribution per unit = 70 - 45 = $25.

Break-even quantity = \frac{200,000}{25} = 8,000 units per year.

examples.problem: A flood wall costs $750,000 to build and $25,000 per year to maintain. It prevents $110,000 of damage per year. Over 30 years at 6%, what is the benefit-cost ratio?
examples.idea: Benefit-cost analysis compares benefits and costs on the same time basis. Convert the annual amounts to present worth with (P/A, i, n) = ((1 + i)^{n} - 1) / (i(1 + i)^{n}), then divide present worth of benefits by present worth of costs. A ratio above 1 means the project is justified.

examples.problem: A machine costs $60,000, costs $4,000 per year to run, and has a salvage value of $8,000 after 10 years. At 9% interest, what is its equivalent uniform annual cost?
examples.idea: Equivalent uniform annual cost spreads every cash flow evenly over the life: the first cost times (A/P), minus the salvage value times the sinking fund factor (A/F), plus the annual operating cost. It lets alternatives with different lives be compared.

examples.problem: A machine costs $75,000 and $5,000 per year to run, plus $2.80 for each unit it makes. It lasts 10 years with no salvage value. Buying the part instead costs $6.50 per unit. At 9% interest, how many units per year make owning the machine break even?
examples.idea: Put owning on an annual basis: the first cost times the capital recovery factor (A/P), plus the fixed annual cost, plus the unit cost times the quantity. Set that equal to the purchase price times the quantity and solve.
examples.steps:
(A/P, 9%, 10) = 0.15582, so the annual cost of owning before any units = 75,000(0.15582) + 5,000 = $16,687.

Each unit made saves 6.50 - 2.80 = $3.70.

Break-even = \frac{16,687}{3.70} = 4,510 units per year.

examples.problem: A signal retiming project costs $94,800 and saves $21,600 per year. What is its simple payback period?
examples.idea: Simple payback is the first cost divided by the annual saving. It ignores interest and anything after the payback date, so it screens projects but does not rank them.

examples.problem: A project costs $145,000 now, returns $33,500 at the end of each year for 6 years and has a salvage value of $15,000 at the end. At 10% interest, what is its net present worth?
examples.idea: Net present worth brings every cash flow to today: the annual returns by the (P/A) factor and the salvage by the (P/F) factor, less the first cost. A positive value means the project earns more than the interest rate.

sections.deep:
Economic analysis compares alternatives on one common measure. Present worth brings everything to today, annual worth spreads everything evenly over the life, and rate of return finds the interest rate at which present worth is zero. Present worth and annual worth always rank alternatives the same way; annual worth is easier when lives differ.

For public projects the benefit-cost ratio divides the present worth of benefits by that of costs, and a ratio above 1 justifies the project. Compare mutually exclusive options incrementally: the extra investment must earn its own keep.
method: Set a common basis: present worth, annual worth or equal study period.
Convert every cash flow of each alternative to that basis with the factors.
Treat costs as negative and salvage as positive, or work consistently in costs.
Choose the highest worth or lowest equivalent cost; for benefit-cost, require a ratio of at least 1.
With unequal lives use annual worth.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: An analysis decides between options. Break-even finds the quantity at which two options cost the same. Benefit-cost divides the value of benefits by the cost. Life-cycle cost adds everything spent over the whole life, moved to one point in time.
needs: Engineering Economics: Time value of money
terms: benefits divided by costs, both in present-worth terms; above 1 means the project pays
the amount today that is equivalent to money received or paid in the future, at a given interest rate
what an asset can be sold for at the end of its life
symbols: uniform amount at the end of each period

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.body:
Real projects have uncertain outcomes. Expected value is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and add. It lets you compare a gamble with a sure thing.

Risk is the spread around that average. Two options can have the same expected value while one is far riskier. A decision tree lays out choices and chances as branches. Work it from the right: compute the expected value at each chance node, then pick the best branch at each decision node.
pitfalls: Probabilities across the outcomes of one event must add to 1.
Forgetting to include costs that are paid whatever the outcome.

example.problem: A bid costs $5,000 to prepare. It has a 25% chance of winning a job worth $60,000 in profit. What is the expected value of bidding?

ideas.title: Expected cost of a risky option
ideas.text: Add to the first cost the probability of failure times the cost of failure, brought to the same time basis. Each option uses its own probability.

ideas.title: Decision trees
ideas.text: Draw decisions as squares and chance events as circles. Work from the right: at each chance node take the expected value of its branches, and at each decision node keep the best branch.

ideas.title: Risk is spread, not just average
ideas.text: Two options with the same expected value can differ in risk. The variance or standard deviation of the outcomes measures that spread, and a risk-averse owner may prefer the option with the lower expected value and the narrower range.

ideas.title: Sensitivity analysis
ideas.text: Change one input at a time and see how much the result moves. The inputs that swing the decision are the ones worth estimating more carefully.

ideas.title: Expected value
ideas.text: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of all outcomes: the sum of each outcome times its probability. Losses enter as negative values, and the probabilities must sum to 1.

examples.problem: A project has a 15% chance of losing $60,000, a 55% chance of earning $35,000 and a 30% chance of earning $110,000. What is its expected value?
examples.idea: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of all outcomes: the sum of each outcome times its probability. Losses enter as negative values, and the probabilities must sum to 1.

examples.problem: A firm estimates a 32% chance of winning a contract that would earn a profit of $415,000. Preparing the proposal costs $23,000, which is lost if the firm does not win. What is the expected value of pursuing it?
examples.idea: Expected value weights each outcome by its probability: the chance of winning times the profit, minus the chance of losing times the cost of the proposal.

sections.deep:
Uncertainty means a decision's outcome is not known in advance. Expected value weights each possible outcome by its probability and is the long-run average if the decision were repeated many times. It is the right measure when stakes are small relative to resources; when a bad outcome would be ruinous, the spread of outcomes matters too.

Decision trees organise sequences of choices and chance events. Sensitivity analysis asks which input assumptions actually change the decision.
method: List every outcome with its probability and check the probabilities sum to 1.
Multiply each outcome by its probability, with losses negative, and add.
For a tree, work from the right: expected values at chance nodes, best branch at decision nodes.
Compare options on expected value, then comment on risk if asked.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: When outcomes are uncertain, weight each one by its probability and add them up. The result, the expected value, is the average outcome if the choice were repeated many times.
